item.title: Sidetrak: a de novo-designed miniprotein targets the kinesin-1 coiled-coil stalk to inhibit MAP7 binding and disrupt mitochondrial transport
item.abstract: The coiled-coil domains of cytoskeletal motors contain regulatory surfaces that offer largely unexploited targets for manipulating intracellular transport. The microtubule-associated protein MAP7 promotes kinesin-1 motor activity, binding a coiled-coil surface that overlaps the TPR docking site (TDS), a regulatory interface involved in autoinhibition. Starting from an AlphaFold3 model of this relatively feature-poor surface, we used BoltzGen to design Sidetrak, a 36-amino acid miniprotein that binds kinesin-1 with nanomolar affinity. Binding requires the TDS and is abolished by mutation of the predicted Sidetrak interface, supporting the modelled local geometry of the targeted coiled-coil region. Sidetrak inhibits MAP7 binding, reduces MAP7-dependent kinesin-1 recruitment to microtubules in cells and causes perinuclear redistribution of mitochondria, a kinesin-1 cargo. Sidetrak binds all three kinesin-1 heavy-chain paralogues, and quantitative interaction proteomics revealed selective association with endogenous kinesin-1 complexes and associated cargo adaptors. These findings demonstrate selective disruption of a motor-MAP interaction by a de novo-designed protein and highlight regulatory coiled-coil surfaces as targets for manipulating intracellular transport. Beyond providing a means to manipulate intracellular transport, this work illustrates the potential of de novo protein design to test structural models of protein interfaces and probe endogenous protein networks to uncover underlying cellular mechanisms.

item.title: Machine learning guided design of strong transcriptional activation domains.
item.abstract: Artificial intelligence has accelerated the design of structured proteins, but it remains difficult to design functional intrinsically disordered proteins because of weak structural constraints and poorly defined sequence-to-function relationships 1 . Activation domains (ADs), transcription factor regions that recruit coactivators, are an excellent test case for the de novo design of intrinsically disordered sequences. ADs are one of the oldest groups of functional intrinsically disordered sequences 2 and designed ADs have applications in synthetic biology, biotechnology, and agriculture. We computationally generated 500,000 candidate sequences that resembled known ADs and predicted AD function with extant machine learning models, including three neural networks. From high-scoring sequences, we selected 18,750 for experimental validation in yeast. Surprisingly, >90% of the 16,770 well-measured sequences function as ADs. Sequences predicted to be active by multiple models were stronger, motivating development of a fast and accurate consensus AD predictor, MADRIGAL. A number of our designed ADs retain functionality across fungi, plants, and human cells. This work illustrates a generalizable paradigm for incorporating sequence-to-function models into the design loop to efficiently generate functional intrinsically disordered sequences.

item.title: Tiled base editing screens uncover rare second-site mutations that rescue a misfolded disease protein.
item.abstract: Therapeutic base editing can directly revert ∼30% of disease-causing missense mutations to the wild-type sequence. One strategy to broaden its reach is to install second-site corrector mutations that improve protein stability or function across multiple pathogenic alleles. Here, we use tiled adenine and cytosine base editing screens to identify such corrector mutations in NPC1, a lysosomal cholesterol transporter whose misfolding causes Niemann-Pick type C disease. Tiling mutagenesis of the endogenous NPC1 locus in haploid human cells carrying the prevalent NPC1 I1061T disease allele, combined with phenotypic reporters for cholesterol transport and protein abundance, uncovered rare intragenic suppressor mutations distributed across multiple domains. Unexpectedly, we identified a promiscuous second-site variant that can correct many different pathogenic NPC1 mutations. These correctors improve protein stability, promote ER exit and lysosomal trafficking, and restore cholesterol clearance in patient-derived fibroblasts and induced neurons. Our results establish in situ base editing screens for the discovery of second-site corrector mutations that are actionable for therapeutic base editing when the original mutation cannot be corrected.

item.title: Disease Modeling of Fabry Disease Cardiomyopathy using Base Editing-Established Isogenic iPSCs and Application of Prime Editing for Gene Correction.
item.abstract:
PURPOSE: Fabry disease (FD) is a genetic disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the alpha-galactosidase A (GLA) gene, resulting in lysosomal accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3). The location of mutations in the GLA gene varies among patients, which causes differences in disease severity and therapeutic responses, highlighting the need for personalized disease models. This study aimed to establish an isogenic human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-based FD cardiomyopathy model to evaluate drug efficacy and to explore the therapeutic potential of prime editing.
METHODS: Two point mutations were introduced into GLA in hiPSCs using adenine and cytosine base editors. Two FD hiPSC lines and isogenic control hiPSCs were differentiated into cardiomyocytes (CMs), followed by disease phenotyping and evaluation of drug efficacy. To suggest an advanced treatment option, the prime editing technique was applied to the FD hiPSCs, followed by analysis of corrected hiPSCs and CMs.
RESULTS: FD phenotypes were confirmed in FD CMs by reduced GLA activity and increased Gb3 accumulation compared with isogenic controls. Treatment with the pharmacological chaperone 1-deoxygalactonojirimycin restored GLA enzyme activity in FD CMs. Additionally, CMs derived from hiPSCs corrected by prime editing exhibited GLA protein levels and enzyme activity comparable to those of the isogenic control, with a decrease in Gb3 accumulation.
CONCLUSIONS: Our results demonstrate that base-edited isogenic hiPSC-CMs provide a personalized platform for evaluating therapeutic efficacy without patient-derived samples. Moreover, genetic correction of GLA via prime editing highlights the potential of gene therapy for FD.

item.title: Base Editing of Hematopoietic Stem Cells Corrects Gain-of-Function Mutations in APDS.
item.abstract: Activated phosphoinositide 3-kinase delta syndrome 1 and 2 (APDS1, APDS2) are rare gain-of-function inborn errors of immunity (IEI) leading to recurrent severe infections, bronchiectasis, lymphoproliferation and lymphoma. APDS1 and APDS2 are caused by mutations in PIK3CD and PIK3R1 respectively, which together encode the subunits of the phosphoinositide 3-kinase  enzyme (PI3K). The only curative therapy is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT), which requires a suitable donor and incurs a significant risk of morbidity and mortality. An adenine base editing strategy was developed to target the most frequent point mutations in APDS1 (p.E1021K, c.3061G>A; ~90% of patients) and APDS2 (c.1425+1G > A; ~50% of patients). Highly efficient correction of the pathogenic point mutation was achieved in patient T cells and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and associated with functional restoration of PI3K signaling, rescue of the activation-induced cell death phenotype and, in APDS2, abrogated expression of the pathogenic splice isoform. Edited HSCs maintained pluripotency and achieved long-term engraftment in immunodeficient mice. A healthy control:APDS1 mixed chimera mouse model suggested that 75% wild-type engraftment generated a wild-type phenotype with respect to T and B cell dysfunction and lymphoproliferation, and thus similar editing efficiencies would be predicted to improve patient clinical phenotype. Together, these data demonstrate successful application of base editing to a gain-of-function IEI, with potential for application in other diseases.

item.title: Redesigning the bacterial envelope: Multi-layered genetic strategies for outer membrane vesicle production.
item.abstract: Bacterial outer membrane vesicles (OMVs) are promising nanoplatforms for therapeutics, vaccines, and bioengineering; however, their industrial translation is constrained by low native yields and strain-dependent heterogeneity. Although static genetic knockouts can enhance vesicle shedding, they often provoke envelope fragility, premature cell lysis, and downstream contamination-creating a severe trade-off between vesicle yield and host cellular fitness. This review systematically outlines genetic strategies to optimise OMV yield, cargo selectivity, and biosafety across four biophysical dimensions: outer membrane layer remodelling, periplasmic waste accumulation and turgor stress, outer membrane-peptidoglycan tether disruption, and multi-layered combinatorial engineering. For each dimension, the molecular mechanisms, comparative merits, and operational bottlenecks are analysed alongside representative biomedical and industrial applications. Finally, we discuss autonomous dynamic circuits for mitigating yield-fitness trade-offs and the prospective role of artificial intelligence (AI)-guided systems design, which remains contingent on suitable datasets and experimental validation. We further consider chassis diversification and standardised orthogonal phenotyping as complementary directions for advancing OMV biomanufacturing. Harnessing these integrated synthetic biology toolkits may facilitate the development of robust and scalable OMV biomanufacturing platforms.

item.title: Multiomic analysis of a pleural mesothelioma organoid biobank defines gene dependencies and therapeutic vulnerabilities
item.abstract: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) remains an incurable cancer with few effective therapeutic options and limited understanding of its targetable dependencies, owing in part to a scarcity of clinically relevant, scalable models. Here, we describe establishment of an annotated biobank of 26 patient-derived PM organoids that faithfully recapitulate the clinical, genomic and histopathological landscapes of their parent tumours, including driver mutations, copy-number alterations and mutational signatures. By integrating these organoid models with a complementary collection of low-passage primary PM cell lines, we generate a functional precision oncology platform for PM. Genome-scale CRISPR-Cas9 screening across 23 patient-derived PM models uncovered 1,150 core fitness genes, including 638 not shared with pan-cancer core essentials, highlighting critical requirements for proteostasis, DNA repair, RNA processing and cell-cycle control. Parallel profiling of 106 compounds across 36 PM models revealed broad therapeutic vulnerabilities in proteostasis, growth signalling and epigenetic regulation. Beyond these shared vulnerabilities, both screens uncovered genotype-specific dependencies and drug responses linked to recurrent PM alterations. This functional map of shared and genotype-specific dependencies establishes patient-derived organoids as a scalable platform for precision therapeutic discovery in pleural mesothelioma

item.title: Molecularly profiling cell-free DNA from cerebrospinal fluid yields quantitative biomarkers to diagnose and monitor breast cancer leptomeningeal carcinomatosis.
item.abstract:
PURPOSE: Leptomeningeal carcinomatosis (LC), the spread of cancer to the fluid-filled spaces of the central nervous system, is an increasingly common and rapidly fatal complication of breast cancer. Standardized clinical diagnostic methods, such as cytology and MRI, have limited accuracy, do not identify therapy-defining mutations, and are not quantitative. Here, we sought to develop the molecular analysis of cell-free DNA in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) as a quantitative tool to diagnose and monitor LC.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: Cell-free DNA from the CSF of 35 breast cancer patients referred for the clinical evaluation of potential LC underwent next-generation sequencing. TrueR sequencing, a duplex-based workflow, was used to suppress false positives during variant discovery. PolkaDot, a novel low-pass whole genome sequencing algorithm, quantitatively mapped genomic instability.
RESULTS: Twenty-three patients were clinically diagnosed with LC, and 12 patients were clinically determined not to have LC. TrueR somatic mutation detection was 78.3% sensitive and 100% specific for clinically confirmed LC and associated with worse overall survival (HR=9.5 [3.5-25.5], P=0.0003). PolkaDot was 87.0% sensitive and 100% specific and predicted worse overall survival (HR=17.5 [6.6-46.9], P=0.0001). Cytology (34.8% sensitive, 100% specific; HR=2.1 [0.6-7.6], P=0.15) and MRI (82.6% sensitive, 50.0% specific; HR=0.9 [0.3-2.5], P=0.76) were not prognostic. Using serial samples, the quantitative monitoring of the mutation molecular burden and genomic instability identified treatment susceptibility and resistance, and disease recurrence.
CONCLUSIONS: CSF cell-free DNA is a minimally invasive biomarker that provides an objective diagnosis of breast cancer LC and personalized molecular profiles for quantitative disease monitoring to support clinical management.
item.journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research

item.title: A Novel Cell-Derived Therapy Reduces Corneal Fluorescein Staining in Preclinical Models of Dry Eye.
item.abstract: Dry eye disease (DED), particularly in the context of Sjögren disease (SjD), remains a significant clinical challenge due to its multifactorial nature and lack of targeted therapies. This study evaluates the therapeutic potential of two novel cell-free biologics-megakaryocyte-like cell (MLC) extract-1 (ME-1) and MLC extract-2 (ME-2)-derived from human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-generated MLCs in preclinical models of DED. MLCs were differentiated from hiPSCs and processed to produce ME-1 via microfluidic device-induced shear stress and ME-2 via freeze-thaw lysis. Protein composition of ME-1, ME-2, and plasma rich in growth factors (PRGF) was analyzed using Luminex multiplex assays. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed in two mouse models: a desiccative stress model and a thrombospondin-1 knockout (TSP1-/-) model of SjD. Corneal fluorescein staining (CFS) scores were used to assess ocular surface damage. ME-1 and ME-2 contained key growth factors associated with corneal healing, at levels comparable to or higher than a PRGF preparation. In the desiccative stress model, ME-1 showed a non-significant reduction in CFS relative to vehicle, while Optimmune® showed a significant reduction relative to vehicle. In the TSP1-/- model, both ME-1 and ME-2 showed reduction of a similar magnitude to PRGF. These findings suggest that hiPSC-derived MLC extracts may improve ocular surface disease signs, as measured by corneal fluorescein staining, in preclinical models of DED. Their derivation from hiPSCs and adaptable cytokine profiles support their potential development as biologic therapies for DED, including SjD-associated dry eye.

item.title: Recognition of the centromere-binding protein Ndc10 by Scm3 HJURP directs Cse4 CENP-A deposition at native centromeres.
item.abstract:
UNLABELLED: Kinetochores connect centromeres to spindle microtubules, ensuring accurate chromosome segregation. Kinetochore assembly at centromeres depends on deposition of CENP-A, a histone H3 variant. Despite considerable progress, how CENP-A is specifically assembled on native centromeres remains an open question. Centromere-specific assembly of CENP-A occurs spontaneously in a cell-free extract system from the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae , but with low efficiency, suggesting that one or more factors are limiting. Here, we show Scm3 HJURP , a specific chaperone for the centromeric histone Cse4 CENP-A , is one such limiting component. The addition of a complex of Scm3, Cse4 and histone H4 strongly stimulates Cse4 assembly in a centromeric DNA sequence- and dose-dependent manner; in addition, improvements in both Cse4 and kinetochore assembly were more prominent in mitotic versus interphase (G1) extracts. Using the complemented cell-free reconstitution system, we show that distinct Scm3 interfaces with Cse4 and with the Ndc10 subunit of the yeast centromere DNA sequence-recognizing CBF3 complex are essential for centromere-specific Cse4 assembly and cell viability. Thus, recognition of Ndc10 directs Scm3-dependent and locus-specific centromeric histone deposition.
SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Accurate chromosome segregation depends on the assembly of kinetochores at centromeres. In budding yeast, centromeres are specified by DNA sequence, but how sequence recognition is coupled to deposition of the centromeric histone Cse4 remains incompletely understood. Using a cell-free assembly system, we show that Scm3 promotes centromeric Cse4 assembly through distinct regions that bind Cse4/H4 and the centromere-binding protein Ndc10. Mutations that disrupt Ndc10 binding impair Cse4 assembly in extracts, reduce Scm3 association with centromeres in cells, and compromise viability. These findings support a mechanism in which a histone chaperone engages a sequence-specific centromere-binding complex to direct centromeric histone assembly.

item.title: Drp-1 Participates in LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation and Microglia-Neuron Interaction Through mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis.
item.abstract: To investigate the role of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp-1) in the process of LPS-induced microglial injury and its initiated neuroinflammation. C57BL/6J mice or BV2 microglia were challenged with LPS, and the behavioral performance and the cell viability were tested, respectively. The expression of Drp-1, inflammatory factors, and key molecules of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway was measured in the mouse hippocampus or in microglia in vitro, together with the abundance of mtDNA. Moreover, the effect of Drp-1 was further explored by siRNA in vitro and its selective inhibitor Mdivi-1 in vivo. Furthermore, a co-culture system of microglia and neurons was used to observe the potential role of cell-free mtDNA in the microglia-neuron crosstalk. Meanwhile, the plasma levels of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) were detected in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In vivo, intraperitoneal injection of LPS could result in anxious-like and depression-like behaviors in mice, together with a significant microglial activation and its related neuroinflammation, mtDNA release, and the imbalanced expression of synaptic plasticity, Drp-1, cGAS, STING, p-STING, and IRF3 in the hippocampus. All these behavioral and neuropathological changes could be reversed by treatment with Mdivi-1. Moreover, LPS-induced behavioral dysfunction and neuropathological injuries were also observed in mice that received hippocampal stereotactic injection of mtDNA. In vitro, besides the detrimental effect of LPS on microglia, our results indicated a crucial role of microglia-derived mtDNA in linking Drp-1-associated mitochondrial dysfunction to LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation, and in the crosstalk between HT22 and BV2 cells. Additionally, the plasma concentration of cf-mtDNA was increased in MDD patients, with a significant positive correlation with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. As a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, the imbalanced expression of Drp-1 participates in LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation via the Drp-1-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis.

item.title: Functional differentiation during rapid degradation of 17β-estradiol by an enriched microbial consortium.
item.abstract: 17β-Estradiol (E2), a potent endocrine-disrupting steroid hormone, poses a serious threat to human and ecological health. However, the functional roles of taxa in microbial consortia during E2 degradation remain unclear. Here, we found that the aerobic enrichment consortium HNE2-16 completely degraded 50 mg/L E2 within 24 h, achieving a remarkably high degradation efficiency reported by now. Estrone (E1), a classical dehydrogenated product of E2, accumulated during the first 12 h and was subsequently depleted, coupled with biomass increase. Moreover, intermediate identification and multi-omics analyses suggested that consortium HNE2-16 contained three E2 degradation pathways, including the estrogen 4,5-seco pathway, D-ring cleavage pathway, and a hypothetical androgen-forming followed by 9,10-seco androgen degradation pathway. Rhodococcus accounted for 4.00-17.07% of the community, harbored and expressed all three pathways. Additionally, the isolate of Rhodococcus was able to degrade all six tested steroid hormones. In contrast, Hyphomicrobium (40.96-49.58%), Dyella (16.01-17.00%), and some minor taxa (0.01-1.61%) harbored and expressed incomplete pathways for E2 degradation, indicating a potential cross-feeding of metabolites within community members. This was consistent with the transformation capacity of their isolates. Pairwise co-culturing of Rhodococcus with Hyphomicrobium and Mycobacterium with Dyella reduced the accumulation of E1 during E2 transformation. Dyella showed growth on the cell-free culture of Rhodococcus after E2 degradation. Besides, novel enzymes Hy-OecA (17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase) and Hy-Fmo (flavin-dependent monooxygenase) from Hyphomicrobium showed conversion capacity on E2 and E1, respectively. Together, these results reveal functional differentiation among enriched taxa during E2 degradation, with Rhodococcus acting as the primary degrader and other taxa playing partial or auxiliary roles in E2 degradation.

item.title: Biofilm-State Probiotics for Seafood Safety: Multifactorial Mechanisms and Emerging Biocontrol Strategies.
item.abstract: Biofilms formed by foodborne pathogens on seafood and processing surfaces can withstand refrigeration, cleaning, and chemical sanitization, allowing them to persist as reservoirs for recurrent product contamination. The antimicrobial and antibiofilm activities of probiotic bacteria, particularly lactic acid bacteria (LAB), are well documented, but the physiological state in which a probiotic is applied has received far less attention. Biofilm-state probiotics (BSPs), defined here as probiotic microorganisms intentionally established as confirmed surface-associated biofilms, occupy the colonizable surface before pathogens arrive, whereas planktonic cells and probiotic-derived preparations such as cell-free supernatants and bacteriocins deliver activity that dilutes, degrades, and must be reapplied. Existing reviews discuss these categories together, making it difficult to determine whether reported activity is attributable to the biofilm state. This review applies an explicit framework separating direct BSP evidence, in which a confirmed probiotic biofilm is challenged with a pathogen, from supporting evidence obtained by other means. Applying it leaves a small body of work. Preformed probiotic biofilms have excluded Listeria monocytogenes, Salmonella Typhimurium, and Escherichia coli O157:H7 from abiotic surfaces; a pre-established Lactiplantibacillus plantarum biofilm suppressed adhesion, motility, and quorum sensing in Vibrio parahaemolyticus; and competitive-exclusion bacteria eliminated L. monocytogenes from five of six drains in a commercial processing plant for 13 weeks. However, no study has compared one strain as biofilm, planktonic cells, and cell-free preparation in a seafood matrix, and none has evaluated food-contact surfaces during production. BSPs therefore remain an emerging platform rather than a validated intervention, requiring standardized biofilm verification, sanitation compatibility, regulatory clarification, and pilot-scale validation.
